name: Manuel Castells
milestone_by_age_26: Earned a doctorate in sociology from the University of Paris in 1967 at age 25 under Alain Touraine and began teaching as an instructor at the University of Paris.
early_history_summary: Castells completed secondary education two years early at 16 and studied law and economics at the University of Barcelona before fleeing Franco's Spain as a political exile to Paris in 1962. He completed his first degree at the Sorbonne in 1964 and earned his doctorate in sociology from the University of Paris in 1967 under Alain Touraine at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales.
family_context_summary: Born to middle-class civil servants in Franco-era Spain; father was a finance inspector and mother an accountant. Grew up in a conservative family in Madrid, Cartagena, and Valencia.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were civil servants with the Spanish Ministry of Finance; no direct connection to sociology or academia.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite institution, Touraine mentorship, political exile, French academia, sociology
evidence_summary: Castells completed secondary education early at 16 and studied law and economics at the University of Barcelona before fleeing Franco's Spain as a political exile to Paris. He earned his doctorate in sociology from the University of Paris in 1967 at age 25 under Alain Touraine, a leading French sociologist who became his mentor. His parents were middle-class civil servants, providing a stable but not privileged background. The political repression he experienced as a student activist catalyzed his academic focus on power and social movements.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class civil servant family in Hellin, Spain; father was a finance inspector, mother an accountant with the Spanish Ministry of Finance.
current_position: University Professor and Wallis Annenberg Chair at USC Annenberg; Professor Emeritus at UC Berkeley; Fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge; served as Spain's Minister of Universities (2020-2021).

trajectory.event: Completed first degree at the Sorbonne after fleeing Franco's Spain as a political exile.
Earned doctorate in sociology from the University of Paris under Alain Touraine and began teaching as instructor.
Published first book 'La Question Urbaine,' translated into 10 languages and became a global classic.
Appointed Professor of Sociology and City Planning at UC Berkeley.
Published first volume of 'The Information Age' trilogy, his most influential work on network society.
Served as Minister of Universities of Spain in the Sanchez government.

name: Gerd Binnig
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; earned a bachelor's degree in physics from Goethe University Frankfurt in 1973 at age 26, but his Nobel Prize-winning invention of the scanning tunneling microscope came in 1981 at age 34.

name: Donna Strickland
milestone_by_age_26: Co-invented chirped pulse amplification (CPA) with Gerard Mourou and published the seminal paper in Optics Communications in October 1985 at age 26, the work that later won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
early_history_summary: Strickland graduated from McMaster University with a BEng in engineering physics in 1981 and joined Gerard Mourou's laser lab at the University of Rochester for her PhD. She was assigned to make Mourou's CPA concept a reality, and they published the groundbreaking paper in 1985 when she was 26.
family_context_summary: Born to a middle-class family in Guelph, Ontario; father was an electrical engineer at General Electric, mother was an English teacher. Father encouraged her interest in science, pointing to lasers as 'the future' during a science museum visit.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an electrical engineer at GE who provided early exposure to science and technology, directly influencing her path toward engineering physics and lasers.
primary_early_advantage_tags: PhD mentor, laser optics, engineering family, University of Rochester, CPA
evidence_summary: Strickland grew up in a middle-class family in Guelph, Ontario, with her father, an electrical engineer, encouraging her interest in science. She graduated from McMaster in 1981 and joined Gerard Mourou's laser lab at the University of Rochester for her PhD. At age 26, she co-invented chirped pulse amplification (CPA) and published the seminal paper in 1985, which later won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics. Her father's engineering background provided early domain exposure, and Mourou's mentorship was the key catalyst for the breakthrough.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Guelph, Ontario; father was an electrical engineer at General Electric, mother was an English teacher at Guelph Collegiate.
current_position: Professor of Physics at the University of Waterloo; Nobel Laureate in Physics (2018); resides in Waterloo, Ontario.

name: Virginia Ruzici
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1978 French Open singles championship at age 23, also winning the doubles title and reaching the mixed doubles final in the same tournament.
early_history_summary: Ruzici started playing tennis at age 8 in her hometown of Campia Turzii, Romania, after being spotted by a local coach while playing soccer. She trained at Dinamo club in Bucharest from age 10, debuted for Romania in the Fed Cup at 18 in 1973, and turned professional in 1975. She won her first WTA titles in 1974 at age 19.
family_context_summary: Born in Campia Turzii, a small industrial town in Romania; father was a footballer who played for the local team, mother was a homemaker. Family moved to Bucharest when she was 10.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a footballer, providing a sports-oriented family environment but no tennis-specific domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: tennis club access, Romanian sports system, peer group, natural athlete, early training
evidence_summary: Ruzici grew up near tennis courts in a small Romanian town and was spotted playing soccer at age 8 by a local coach. She trained at Dinamo club in Bucharest from age 10 and debuted for Romania in the Fed Cup at 18. She won the French Open in 1978 at age 23, becoming one of the few Eastern European players of her era to win a Grand Slam. Her family was not wealthy, and she faced significant financial and travel constraints as an Eastern European athlete behind the Iron Curtain.
starting_point: Born in Campia Turzii, Romania; father was a footballer, mother a homemaker; family moved to Bucharest when she was 10 to access better training.
current_position: Tennis manager for Simona Halep; lives in Paris, France; retired from professional tennis in 1987.

trajectory.event: Debuted for Romania in the Fed Cup, reaching the semifinals in their first-ever appearance.

name: Ulyana Lopatkina
milestone_by_age_26: Promoted to principal dancer at the Mariinsky Theatre in 1995 at age 22, after winning the Vaganova-Prix competition in 1990 and joining the company upon graduation in 1991.
early_history_summary: Lopatkina moved from Kerch, Crimea, to Leningrad alone at age 10 to train at the Vaganova Ballet Academy under Natalia Dudinskaya. Despite being initially assessed as having average ability, she won the Vaganova-Prix competition at 16, joined the Mariinsky Ballet in 1991, and was promoted to principal dancer in 1995 at age 22.
family_context_summary: Born in Kerch, Crimea; father was a production manager at a shipbuilding facility, mother an economist. Mother wanted her to become a ballerina and supported her moving to Leningrad alone at age 10.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family ballet background; mother had a life-long dream of ballet that she projected onto Ulyana, but no professional domain expertise was transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Vaganova Academy, Mariinsky Theatre, Dudinskaya mentorship, St. Petersburg ballet, early training
evidence_summary: Lopatkina moved from Kerch, Crimea, to Leningrad alone at age 10 to train at the Vaganova Ballet Academy under Natalia Dudinskaya, a legendary Kirov ballerina. Despite being initially assessed as having average ballet ability, she won the Vaganova-Prix competition at 16 and joined the Mariinsky Ballet upon graduation in 1991. She was promoted to principal dancer at 22 in 1995. Her mother, an economist, had dreamed of ballet and supported the sacrifice of sending her daughter away. The Vaganova-Mariinsky pipeline was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Kerch, Crimea; father was a production manager at a shipyard, mother an economist; moved to Leningrad alone at age 10 to train at the Vaganova Ballet Academy.
current_position: Retired prima ballerina of the Mariinsky Theatre (1991-2017); resides in St. Petersburg, Russia.

name: Robin Warren

name: Sadako Sasaki
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; died at age 12 in 1955 from leukemia caused by atomic bomb radiation. Her symbolic significance as a peace icon was established posthumously through her classmates' efforts, not by age 26.
early_history_summary: Sasaki was two years old when the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima in 1945. She survived apparently uninjured but developed acute leukemia ten years later. While hospitalized, she folded over 1,000 origami cranes before dying at age 12 in October 1955. Her story became a global peace symbol posthumously through her classmates' fundraising campaign.
family_context_summary: Born in Hiroshima in 1943; father Shigeo was a barber. Family was exposed to the atomic bomb at their home 1.6 km from ground zero; grandmother died in the bombing. Family struggled with financial hardship and food scarcity after the war.
evidence_summary: Sasaki was two years old when the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima in 1945 and died of radiation-induced leukemia at age 12 in 1955. While hospitalized, she folded over 1,000 origami cranes based on a Japanese legend. Her symbolic significance as a peace icon was established posthumously through her classmates' efforts to build the Children's Peace Monument in Hiroshima, completed in 1958. The fame and recognition arrived after her death, not by age 26. She never reached age 26.

He bought his first racing bike with money earned from farm work and joined local youth cycling clubs. He competed in the 1980 Olympics and turned professional in 1981, immediately achieving second place at Paris-Nice and La Fleche Wallonne in his first season.
family_context_summary: Born in Bergen op Zoom, Netherlands; grew up on a farm in Hoogerheide. Earned money for his first racing bike by doing farm work for his uncle. Later married Corinne, daughter of cycling legend Raymond Poulidor.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family cycling background documented before his own career; his connection to cycling royalty came through marriage to Raymond Poulidor's daughter, not through parental inheritance.

evidence_summary: Van der Poel grew up in Hoogerheide on the Dutch-Belgian border, a region with deep cycling culture and ideal training terrain. He bought his first racing bike with money earned from farm work and joined local youth cycling clubs. name: Denis Law
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Ballon d'Or as European Footballer of the Year in 1964 at age 24, the only Scottish player ever to win the award, having already set three British transfer records and earned international caps for Scotland from age 18.
early_history_summary: Law was scouted by Huddersfield Town at 15 and made his professional debut at 16 in 1956. He became Scotland's youngest international in 60 years at 18 in 1958. He was transferred for British record fees to Manchester City (1960, age 20), Torino (1961, age 21), and Manchester United (1962, age 22). At United he scored 46 goals in one season and won the Ballon d'Or in 1964.
family_context_summary: Born in Aberdeen, Scotland; youngest of seven children; father was a fisherman. Grew up in a council flat and went barefoot until age 12. First pair of football boots was a birthday gift from a neighbor at age 16.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family football background; father was a fisherman. No parental domain expertise in football was transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bill Shankly mentorship, poverty, football obsession, Scottish football, Huddersfield Town
evidence_summary: Law grew up in extreme poverty in Aberdeen, the youngest of seven children of a fisherman, going barefoot until 12 and receiving his first football boots at 16 from a neighbor. He was scouted by Huddersfield Town at 15, debuted at 16, and became Scotland's youngest international in 60 years at 18. Bill Shankly's mentorship at Huddersfield was transformative, building his physical strength and overseeing his development. He won the Ballon d'Or at 24 in 1964, the only Scottish player ever to do so, after setting three British transfer records.
starting_point: Born in Aberdeen, Scotland; youngest of seven children; father was a fisherman; grew up in a council flat and went barefoot until age 12.
current_position: Died January 17, 2025 at age 84 in Cheshire, England; final role: Manchester United legend, TV pundit, and founder of the Denis Law Legacy Trust.
